scores.design: Bounded Fleet — compliance-boundary cards, skill-level specialists, one door, one release id
scores.fatal_flaw: It refuses the ask and then still pays for it. The fleet it ships is four compliance boundaries with every finer specialist demoted to a Skill Pack (its own G16 gate exists to enforce that), so 'specialised agents with specialised tools' becomes one Door hop plus developer-message swaps inside one card — while the Door it adds puts a NEW system prefix, and therefore a new prompt-cache miss, in front of every unknown inbound caller that Tier-0 cannot route. The amortisation that is supposed to hide that miss is mis-grounded in code: it claims to extend 'the existing boot warm in bot.py:2455-2510 (_warm_llm_service)', but _warm_llm_service is at D:\Hackathon\backend\voice\bot.py:2586 and sends no request at all — it constructs a throwaway KeepAliveAzureLLMService to pay a 2.46s class-init once per process. The only request-sending warm, prewarm_shared_client in D:\Hackathon\backend\voice\llm_pool.py:174, sends 'Reply with: ok' and warms TLS/HTTP, not a prefix. Its proposed warm call ('the exact system prefix with max_tokens=1') is the exact call llm_pool.py:137-141 documents as a 400 on gpt-5.x ('max_(completion_)tokens=1 makes gpt-5.x return 400 "could not finish the message"'). So the C1 story rests on a mechanism that does not exist yet and on provider prefix-cache behaviour that nothing in this tree has ever measured — no voice path reads a cached-token count (D:\Hackathon\backend\voice\crm_sink.py:1384 reads Anthropic's cache_read_input_tokens, never Azure's prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens).
scores.strongest_idea: Eval caching keyed by content hash with honest provenance: eval_reports.content_key = hash(card_hash, flow_hash, sorted skill_version_ids, grader_version), gate G20 letting G7/G8 pass on a stored passing report and reporting it as 'pass · cached r-…' — never as 'skipped' — with the two conditions stated as load-bearing (grader_version inside the key; fixtures graded on tool calls and CRM rows, not transcripts). It is the only mechanism in the three that makes verification cost track what changed rather than how many specialists exist, and it lands on tables that already exist (sql/14_agent_factory.sql). Runner-up: G16 boundary_distinct plus the studio's 'Promote to card' affordance — a principled, legible brake on card proliferation that neither other design has.

scores.design: Ensemble — many cards authored, one bundle compiled
scores.fatal_flaw: G-E4, the reserved-node-key ceiling — the design's headline capability is gated behind its riskiest, least reversible phase. Flattening N subgraphs into one compiled graph puts every member's nodes in one registry, and D:\Hackathon\backend\voice\tools.py still transitions by NAME: _node(name) at tools.py:422 is a flat dict lookup (`factory = nodes.get(name)`; unknown name logs and returns None, i.e. 'stay here'), and begin_negotiate/begin_dispute/begin_wrap_up/return_to_position all name reserved keys. So exactly one member may own each RESERVED_NODE_KEY, and a second collections-shaped specialist (Hardship, Lapse) cannot own negotiate_ptp or wrap_up until Phase 5 rewrites the name-based transitions — the phase the design itself calls 'the heavy, less reversible tail'. Phases 0-4 therefore ship a fleet that holds one collections-shaped specialist. Secondary, and cheap to fix but unaddressed: the compiled prefix is door prompt + door guardrails + door persona, and D:\Hackathon\backend\voice\natural.py:182-184 is where guardrail_rules go into the system message verbatim — a specialist's compliance guardrails have nowhere to live in this design and would degrade into an evictable developer block. The compiler already builds the prefix at publish, so it can and must union every member's guardrail rules into prefix_text and keep it byte-identical.
scores.strongest_idea: Separating the authoring unit from the runtime unit: many specialist cards on a canvas, one compiled Bundle at runtime, so a hop is a replace_developer('ACTIVE SPECIALIST', …) plus a grant pointer change — mechanically identical to the skill swap that already survives a 30-turn call (voice/tools.py:2826-2827 replace_developer(SKILL_BODY_PREFIX, …), agent_core/skills/runtime.py:1-6). A hop cannot cost a prompt-cache miss because the system bytes never change, which is the only C1 answer in the three that does not depend on unmeasured provider behaviour. Paired with it: moving the mission briefing out of the system prompt (D:\Hackathon\backend\voice\bot.py:531-579 appends mission_mod.briefing and then string-replaces 'inbound collections voice agent') into a developer block — that is a latency FIX, not a neutral change, because today every outbound call has a per-borrower system prefix and therefore no cross-call cache at all. And the 'Flattened view' toggle rendering the compiled graph read-only in the existing FlowCanvas is the best authorability idea in the three: the author sees exactly what the borrower will traverse.

scores.design: Sealed Fleet — Door, Specialists, one version per call
scores.fatal_flaw: The amortisation costs more than the thing it amortises, and it is aimed at a cache hit this codebase has never observed. Every inbound call fires 'one tiny inference per non-entry member' against the same Azure/vLLM deployment that is serving the audio path (runtime_model step 3), so a 6-member fleet pays 5 extra prefills of a 2.5-4k-token prefix per call, forever, for a provider-side cache with a best-effort 5-10 minute TTL. On a fixed on-prem serving stack those prefills compete for the same scheduler slots and KV blocks as the live turn — the mechanism meant to hide the hop is the most likely cause of the slo_miss its own fleet canary would roll back for (VOICE_SLO_MS=800, agent_core/canary.py:27, against a documented 'LLM turn p50 ~1.6s' in voice/tts_pool.py). Bounded's per-worker periodic keep-warm does the same job at O(members × workers / 4 min) instead of O(members × calls). Two supporting hazards it does not price: its swap mechanism is role_message via LLMUpdateSettingsFrame, and D:\Hackathon\backend\voice\amd.py:465-473 records a production incident (VS-4D8667B522) where exactly that frame pushed the conversation's system instruction onto a sibling classifier LLM, which then classified its own greeting as VOICEMAIL — mid-call role_message swaps turn a start-of-call frame into a per-hop broadcast, and every sibling LLM in the pipeline now needs the AMD guard; and its Phase 0(b) inserts interaction_handoffs rows with reason='specialist_route'-class values, but sql/04_interactions.sql:71 has a CHECK constraint limiting reason to eight values, none of which are those (Ensemble is the only design that names this CHECK in its migration).
scores.strongest_idea: The hop instrumentation contract, and the fact-only packet schema behind it. hop.ttfb_ms p50/p95, hop.cached_tokens ratio from usage.prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens, hop.cover_ms (bridge-line audio duration minus first-token latency — positive means the miss was hidden), hops_per_call and misroute_rate (target hands back within two turns), with slo_miss applied to hop turns specifically so a badly authored fleet rolls itself back. cover_ms in particular is the only metric proposed in any of the three that measures whether the amortisation actually worked rather than asserting it. Alongside it: PacketField as a Literal with no member for offer, waiver, amount or contact time, so a decision cannot cross a hop by schema rather than by convention; and Phase 0(a), a real verified fail-open fix — voice/tools.py:2781-2787 builds the handoff allowlist from defaults.card_for(bot_id) and sets allowlist=None on KeyError, while agent_core/tools/domain.py:1026 treats None as 'any target permitted', so a tenant card today can hand off anywhere.

best: Ensemble — many cards authored, one bundle compiled
graft: WHY ENSEMBLE AND NOT BOUNDED, despite Bounded's higher raw total (35 vs 34): all three designs put a Door in front of inbound, so all three add at least one hop to every inbound call. In Bounded and Sealed that hop changes the system prefix and therefore costs a prompt-cache miss on the first minute of the call; in Ensemble it costs nothing by construction. Nothing in this repo has ever measured a prompt-cache hit on the voice path (crm_sink.py:1384 reads Anthropic's cache_read_input_tokens; Azure's prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens is read nowhere), and voice/tts_pool.py records 'the LLM turn (p50 ~1.6s) dominates the turn budget' against VOICE_SLO_MS=800. Betting the door hop on an unmeasured provider cache is a bigger production risk than betting on a local, testable refactor of _node() name-based transitions. Ensemble also gives the product owner the fleet they asked for; Bounded's own last risk states that it refuses that ask on purpose. Ensemble wins on the condition that it absorbs the grafts below — most of its constraint deficits are omissions with named fixes, not structural.

GRAFT 1 (from Sealed Fleet — removes Ensemble's fatal flaw): node-key namespacing <slug>/<key> at compile time plus _node(name) resolving inside the ACTIVE specialist's namespace, and G18's use of voice/node_contracts.py NODE_REQUIRED on the handoff entry node so an authored specialist without a wrap_up is never unleaveable. This dissolves G-E4 outright: every member can own negotiate_ptp and wrap_up, the built-in begin_* transitions keep working, and the multi-specialist capability stops being gated behind Ensemble's Phase 5. Do it in Phase 1, not Phase 5 — it is the single highest-value reordering available.

GRAFT 2 (from Sealed Fleet — ship before anything else, independent of the design): Phase 0(a). voice/tools.py:2781-2787 builds the handoff allowlist from agent_core.cards.defaults.card_for(bot_id) and sets allowlist=None on KeyError; agent_core/tools/domain.py:1026 is `if allowlist is not None and target not in allowlist`, so None permits any target. bot_runtime.py:945-949 already does it correctly from bundle['agentCard']. Read the allowlist from the published bundle on the voice path too. This is a live fail-open, not a design decision.

GRAFT 3 (from Sealed Fleet): the hop instrumentation contract — hop.ttfb_ms p50/p95, cached-token ratio, hop.cover_ms (bridge audio duration minus first-token latency), hops_per_call, misroute_rate, with canary slo_miss evaluated on hop turns specifically. Ensemble ASSERTS cache survival across hops and measures nothing, which makes its strongest claim its least falsifiable. Add prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens to crm_sink's usage capture (it reads only cache_read_input_tokens today) so the claim can be proven on the first canary rather than believed.

GRAFT 4 (from Sealed Fleet): G17 door_readonly as a concrete tool allowlist on the door card {verify_identity, get_customer_context, capture_call_goal, handoff_to_agent, search_knowledge_base, set_contact_preference, add_customer_note, escalate_to_human}, plus G20 voice_continuity requiring mouth.introduce_as whenever a member's voice differs. Ensemble's G-E3 only requires verify_identity somewhere on the path to a write node; it never forbids the door itself holding create_promise_to_pay. Also take Sealed's rule that a handoff FAILS if the target lacks a human_gate the source has for the same tool — Ensemble's G-E8 merges strictest-wins at compile, which is the same intent, but Sealed's phrasing catches the laundering case explicitly.

GRAFT 5 (from Sealed Fleet): consult_agent off the audio path — an internal-channel card answering a task row via agent_core/mcp_http/tasks.py enqueue/claim/finish, returning a task_id immediately and delivering the answer later through inject_developer. Ensemble explicitly says no parallel consultation between specialists and is right to for the mouth; this gives the owner real agent-to-agent communication (supervisor-brief, hardship-assessor, doc-verifier) at zero audio-path cost, which is the honest way to satisfy 'agents communicate among themselves'.

GRAFT 6 (from Bounded Fleet): the Prefix Warmer as a PER-WORKER PERIODIC keep-warm — publish-time prime plus a refresh every ~4 minutes for each active production deployment on this voice worker — instead of Sealed's per-call closure warm. Ensemble needs this too, because its whole point is that prefix_text is byte-identical per DEP and therefore warmable once per worker rather than once per call. Take Bounded's on-prem note with it: vLLM prefix caching is process-local, so the warm and the serve must be the same engine worker. Correct one detail before implementing: use max_output_tokens=16, not 1 — llm_pool.py:137-141 documents that 1 returns a 400 on gpt-5.x, and _warm_llm_service (bot.py:2586) is a class-init warm that sends no request, so this is new code, not an extension.

GRAFT 7 (from Bounded Fleet): eval caching by content_key = hash(card_hash, flow_hash, sorted skill_version_ids, grader_version) with gate G20 reporting 'pass · cached r-…' and never 'skipped'. Ensemble's incremental-eval story depends on scope tags on eval_tasks and on a changed-member diff; a content hash is stronger because it cannot drift from what actually changed, and grader_version in the key means a grader fix correctly invalidates every cached report. Keep Bounded's two stated conditions as acceptance criteria, not comments: grader_version inside the key, and fixtures graded on tool calls and CRM rows rather than transcripts.

GRAFT 8 (from Bounded Fleet): G16 boundary_distinct plus the studio's 'this is a skill, not a card / Promote to card' affordance. Ensemble makes cards cheap to author and has no brake, but in Ensemble every card is a permanent tax on the compiled prefix, the ensemble publish set and the reserved-key namespace. G16 gives a compliance officer a principled, legible answer to 'I want a PTP specialist card' — and Ensemble is exactly the design that can then say yes cheaply when the boundary is real.

GRAFT 9 (from Bounded Fleet): card.memory.max_hops_per_call (default 2) with an authored line on a refused hop, and the Door 'Who answers this?' simulator plus door fixtures in the fleet suite. Ensemble's compiled edges make ping-pong authorable and it names no cap; Sealed caps at 3 and measures misroute_rate. Take the cap, the authored refusal line, and the simulator — the simulator is the screen that stops a Tier-0 misroute turning a zero-hop call into a one-hop call.

GRAFT 10 (from Bounded Fleet's thesis, applied to Ensemble's compiler — this is the fix for Ensemble's guardrail hole): union every member's guardrail rules into the compiled prefix_text at publish time. voice/natural.py:182-184 puts guardrail_rules(guardrails, channel='voice') verbatim into the system message and the docstring says it 'KEEPS the authored prompt and every compliance guardrail verbatim'. Ensemble's prefix is door-only, which would silently demote a specialist's compliance text to an evictable developer block. Because the prefix is compiled once at publish, the union stays byte-identical per DEP and costs nothing at runtime — count it against G-E5's 800-token budget (agent_core/skills/lint.py:10).

GRAFT 11 (from Ensemble's own migration, to keep): the interaction_handoffs.reason CHECK-constraint widening. sql/04_interactions.sql:71 limits reason to eight values; Ensemble is the only design that names this. Whatever else is grafted, do not drop it, or Phase 0's first handoff row fails on insert.
unverified_claims: Sealed Fleet: 'roughly +150-400 ms time-to-first-token cold on a GPT-4o-class deployment; roughly +30-80 ms when the prefix was warmed'. No measurement of prompt-cache hit/miss TTFT exists in this tree. The only LLM latency figures recorded anywhere are voice/tts_pool.py's 'LLM turn (p50 ~1.6s)' and bot.py:2586's 2.46s class-init.

Bounded Fleet: 'the hit/miss delta on the voice deployment is roughly 100-300 ms TTFT' on a 2-3k prefix. Self-flagged ('measure; do not assume') and still unsupported by any code or report in the repo.

All three: that Azure/OpenAI prompt caching is being hit at all today. No voice code reads a cached-token count — backend/voice/crm_sink.py:1384 records usage.cache_read_input_tokens (Anthropic's field name) via sink.usage.record_llm; Azure's usage.prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens is read nowhere in the backend. There is therefore zero evidence that any Habibi voice call has ever registered a prompt-cache hit, which makes every hit/miss delta in all three designs a projection.

Ensemble: 'the system message bytes are identical before and after the hop, and identical across calls on the same DEP, so the cached prefix survives every hop'. The system-message half is verifiable by construction; the assumption underneath it — that changing the tool schema set per node does not invalidate the provider's cached prefix — is not verified. Today every authored node already changes NodeConfig.functions (flows_dynamic.py:415-451), and nothing measures whether that costs a hit.

Ensemble: carry='summary' costs '~600-900 ms summarization' overlapped by a bridge line. LLMSummarizeContextFrame is queued at backend/voice/bot.py:1506-1512 but its latency is not recorded anywhere; the 600-900 ms figure has no source in the repo.

Sealed Fleet (also assumed by Bounded and Ensemble for voice_change edges): 'a TTSUpdateSettingsFrame is queued after the bridge line — no measurable cost, Azure TTS voice is per request'. TTSUpdateSettingsFrame appears NOWHERE in this codebase. backend/voice/tts_pool.py documents that the Azure SpeechSynthesizer is constructed once in start() with a websocket pre-opened exactly once, that touching that connection mid-call has already produced a 41s synthesizer deadlock after a barge-in, and that a cold re-handshake costs ~1.5s. Mid-call voice switching is entirely unproven here and is the least safe of the three hop dimensions.

Sealed Fleet: 'sub-millisecond LocalBus dispatch in-process or one Redis RTT (1-3 ms LAN)'. No benchmark exists; backend/voice/mesh_bus.py's _LocalBus is a hand-rolled asyncio queue and the RedisBus path is publish-only (mesh_bus.py:42-47 deliberately never calls RedisBus.start()).

Sealed Fleet: that warming the whole closure at call start is affordable. N-1 extra prefill requests per call against the same deployment serving the audio path is asserted as an amortisation with no capacity, TPM or GPU-scheduler analysis, and on vLLM those prefills contend for the same scheduler and KV blocks as the live turn.

Bounded Fleet: per-hop cost breakdown 'bundle load ~10-30 ms, grant build <1 ms, flow compile ~10-30 ms, registry rebuild <5 ms'. None of these is timed anywhere. build_tools constructs ~35 tool closures in one pass (voice/tools.py:2881-2919) and flows_dynamic compiles a factory per node; neither has an instrument.

Bounded Fleet: 'send the exact system prefix … with max_tokens=1 on the voice LLM'. Contradicted by backend/voice/llm_pool.py:137-141, which documents that max_(completion_)tokens=1 makes gpt-5.x return 400 'could not finish the message' and left the first real turn cold. Use 16.

Bounded Fleet: 'Extends the existing boot warm in bot.py:2455-2510 (_warm_llm_service) from one bundle to the active fleet.' _warm_llm_service is at bot.py:2586 and issues no request — it constructs a throwaway KeepAliveAzureLLMService to pay a measured 2.46s process-wide class init. Prefix warming is entirely new code, not an extension.

Sealed Fleet: 'voice/llm_pool.py (already a shared keep-alive client with prewarm)' used as the base for closure warming. prewarm_shared_client (llm_pool.py:174) sends the literal prompt 'Reply with: ok' — it warms TLS/HTTP and the SDK client, not any prefix.

Sealed Fleet: 'NodeConfig.role_message … delivered by LLMUpdateSettingsFrame, which is how role_message already works.' Corroborated only indirectly, and the corroboration is a warning: backend/voice/amd.py:465-473 names LLMUpdateSettingsFrame as the frame that leaked the flow's system instruction onto the AMD classifier LLM (incident VS-4D8667B522), which then classified its own greeting script as VOICEMAIL. Turning a start-of-call frame into a per-hop broadcast means every sibling LLM service in the pipeline needs the same _CONTEXT_MUTATING guard; no design accounts for this.

Sealed Fleet: whether FlowManager accepts an LLMSwitcher in Pipecat 1.6.0, which gates per-card models under the flows backend. Self-flagged as unverified; BusBridgeProcessor is likewise absent from this tree — voice/workers/insurance.py's own docstring says 'Until the main collections pipeline is fully BusBridge-based, activation is …', i.e. the bridge does not exist yet. LLMWorker, LLMWorkerActivationArgs, activate_worker, RedisBus and AsyncQueueBus DO exist and are used (insurance.py:34, 101-103, 197-202).

All three: the eval-cost arithmetic ('today 12 specialists × (regression + redteam + canary) = 36 full suites'; 'marginal cost of a specialist = seconds'). No suite runtime, cost or LLM-call count is recorded anywhere in the repo, so the sub-linearity claims are structural arguments, not measurements.

Sealed Fleet and Ensemble: that replacing eval/run.py's bot_id_for_suite name-match fixes 'insurance-v1 reporting itself untested'. agent_core/eval/run.py:14-34 documents that this was ALREADY fixed downstream in the Evals tab, and argues that NULL is the truthful owner because a suite is genuinely one-to-many across cards (nine cards name eval-regression-collections). A fleet/door owner may be a better answer, but the stated benefit is stale.

Ensemble: 'one extra LLM call, acceptable off-audio' for the WhatsApp same-turn handoff (Bounded and Sealed make the same move). No latency budget for the text path is documented anywhere, and per repo memory the api/bot_worker root logger has no handler, so regressions on that path are currently invisible — Bounded is the only design that names this as a phase prerequisite.
